thread.title: CNBC’s Cramer says stocks are ‘opening up huge on nothing’, sees signs of ‘classic bear market’ - MarketWatch

author: Mark DeCambre
title: CNBC’s Cramer says stocks are ‘opening up huge on nothing’, sees signs of ‘classic bear market’ - MarketWatch
text:
‘Talk about classic bear-market behavior. We crater all week and then we open up huge on nothing, but because we are so oversold it is hard to let things go.’ Jim Cramer, CNBC Are we in bear market or something more benign?
That’s the crucial question bedeviling a number of investors, including CNBC personality Jim Cramer, lately. This even as the Dow Jones Industrial Average was trading more than 350 points higher, with the S&P 500 SPX, +1.47% and the Nasdaq Composite Index COMP, +1.87% both enjoying gains of better than 1% in early trade .
In a Monday tweet, Cramer appeared to suggest that if the current dynamic walks like a duck and talks like a duck … then it’s bear. In other words, if the characteristics of a bear market are on display then the market should consider that one may be at hand.
Indeed, by some measures more than 200 of the S&P 500 index’s components and 10 of the Dow’s 30 constituents are in a bear market, down at least 20% from a recent bull-market peak, according to FactSet data.
All of the so-called FAANGs, the quintet of growthy stocks — Facebook Inc. FB, +3.89% , Apple Inc. AAPL, +0.68% , Amazon.com Inc. AMZN, +5.05% , Netflix Inc. NFLX, +0.64% and Google parent Alphabet Inc. GOOG, +2.06% GOOGL, +2.20% — that had helped to power this current nearly decade-long bull market are in bear market. Bitcoin BTCUSD, -7.49% , arguably the ultimate risk asset, is down 41% this month.
To many strategists questioning whether the market is engulfed in bearishness amounts to a pedantic, navel-gazing exercise. That is because, beyond the rule of thumb regarding the degree to which an asset must fall to qualify for bear-market status, there is no ultimate arbiter of corrective market phases, such as corrections (declines of at least 10%) and bear markets.
For many investors, real money has been lost, and it isn’t clear when the bloodletting will subside.
The CNBC personality, who co-founded the financial-news site TheStreet, is best known for a 2007 tirade in which he said of the Fed : “They know nothing!” That was in reference to his view that the Fed was ignoring the severity of the asset bubble whose demise was collapsing global financial markets and the U.S. recession that would ensue.
Tomi Kilgore contributed to this report.
